title: Classes are useful for grouping related data and behavior together.
body: Classes are not something you should use indiscriminately. They are best used as a single design unit when data of the same type and the actions that handle that data are repeated.
detail: Therefore, it is important to have criteria for determining whether to group only the data or to include the actions as well. For example, if a `Card` has properties such as `title`, `level`, and `answer`, and you also need to check whether an answer is correct, grouping them into a class makes the code easier to read. Conversely, if you’re simply calculating a single value once, a function alone may be sufficient.

title: Distinguishing Between Instance Variables and Class Variables
body: An instance variable is a value held by each individual object, while a class variable is defined at the class level and can be used as a value shared by multiple objects.
detail: It is important to distinguish between the two to avoid confusing object-specific values with shared values. Beginners should first treat values attached to `self`—such as `self.name`—as instance variables. Conversely, values defined directly within a class may be default settings or shared values referenced by all objects, so you must be careful about whether they are shared when modifying them.

title: Inheritance is a relationship in which a child inherits features from its parent.
body: Inheritance is a structure in which a child class inherits and uses the attributes and methods of a parent class.
detail: Common functionality is placed in the parent class, while the child class can modify only the parts that differ. As a beginner, you should start by understanding the process of inheriting functionality from the parent class. For example, if the `Animal` class has a `speak` method and `Dog` inherits from `Animal`, then `Dog` objects can also use `speak`.

title: "override" and "super" are used to modify or extend parent functionality
body: "Override" refers to redefining a method in a child class that has the same name as one in the parent class. "super()" is used when you want to use the parent class's implementation.
detail: These two concepts often appear together in an inheritance hierarchy when a child class modifies or extends the functionality of a parent class. If a child class wants to completely rewrite a parent class’s functionality, it can recreate a method with the same name. When you want to add only certain parts while retaining the parent’s initialization or common processing, you’ll see code like `super().__init__`.

title: dataclass makes it easy to create classes that group data together
body: @dataclass is a tool that reduces repetitive code—such as __init__—in data-centric classes. Simply defining the fields makes it easier to create objects.
detail: Therefore, it is well-suited for models that hold values, such as cards, settings, and progress states. A structure that holds values such as `title`, `level`, and `answer`—like `Card`—can be a good fit for `dataclass`. It’s important to understand that `dataclass` is not a syntax that replaces all aspects of OOP, but rather a convenience feature designed to make classes used for storing data concise and easy to read.

title: A class isn't always the right answer
body: While classes are great for organizing structure, there’s no need to turn every simple calculation or one-time task into a class. In fact, functions or dictionaries and lists may be easier to read for simple tasks.
detail: Beginners should first see if they can solve the problem using functions, dictionaries, or lists, and consider using a class only when the same data structure and related behavior recur. Using classes too early can increase the number of files and the complexity of filenames, which can actually make the code harder to read. Therefore, classes shouldn’t be used just because they look cool; instead, they should be viewed as a tool to be used when there’s a need to organize recurring structures.
